title: Delaware PIC — Personal or Private Interest 1991-2023
text:
PERSONAL OR PRIVATE INTEREST
1991-2023
23-39—Personal or Private Interest: [Employee] has been [a State official] since January
2022. Among other things, he is responsible for supervising, directing and accounting for
the administration and operation of the Department, its offices, functions and employees.
Those job duties include entering into contracts, hiring personnel, establishing appropriate
regulations and preparing an annual budget.
[The private interest] is a non-profit organization. [One of their programs is licensed
by the Employee’s department].
[Employee] asked the Commission if accepting a role as a [non-profit] trustee would
create a conflict of interest with his State job duties.
A. In their official capacity, state employees or officials may not review or
dispose of matters if they have a personal or private interest in a matter
before them. 29 Del. C. § 5805(a)(1).
A personal or private interest in a matter is an interest which tends to impair a
person’s independence of judgment in the performance of the person’s duties with respect
to that matter.” As a matter of law, a person has a personal or private interest if any
decision “with respect to the matter would result in a financial benefit or detriment to accrue
to the person or a close relative to a greater extent” than others similarly situated or if “the
person or a close relative has a financial interest in a private enterprise which would be
affected” by a decision on the matter to a greater or lesser degree than others similarly
situated. ‘Close relative’ is defined as “a person's parents, spouse, children (natural or
adopted) and siblings of the whole and half-blood.”
A personal or private interest is not limited to narrow definitions such as “close
relatives” and “financial interest.” Instead, it recognizes that a State official can have a
“personal or private interest” outside those limited parameters. It is a codification of the
common law restriction on government officials. When there is a personal or private
interest, the official is to recuse from the outset and even neutral and unbiased statements
are prohibited. Officials subject to the State Code of Conduct often argue, as is the case
here, that there can be no conflict of interest because [Employee]’s status as a Trustee
would not result in “a financial benefit or detriment to accrue to [him] or a close relative.”
That reasoning was flawed. The legal parameters of § 5805(a)(1) are not defined by §
5805(a)(2). First, the Code of Conduct has a clear and specific definition section. Second,
within the clear text of § 5805(a)(1), the second sentence reads “a personal or private
interest is one which tends to impair independence of judgment. . . Thus, within that
provision the law spells out what constitutes a “personal or private interest.” Third, the
Delaware Supreme Court has affirmed an interpretation of § 5805(a)(1) independent of §
5805(a)(2). Fourth, the Commission has held that § 5805(a)(1) is a codification of the
common law restriction on public officials having a personal or private interest. That is
because conflict of interest statutes generally do not abrogate common law conflict of
interest principles.
Statutory interpretation also leads to the same result. When the General Assembly
evidenced its intent for the prohibition to refer only to financial interest, it specifically used
1

that term, which has a very precise statutory definition. In other instances, the Code of
Conduct makes no reference to financial interests. If the General Assembly had meant for
all of the restrictions to be limited to financial interests, it clearly could have done so.
Moreover, to read the Code as limited to pecuniary or financial interests would ignore the
broader statutory language, making broader terms such as “any interest” have no meaning.
The rules of statutory construction require that all words and phrases be given meaning.
Consequently, the Commission did not agree with the statutory interpretation set forth in
your Request Letter stating that conflicts of interest only arise out of pecuniary gain.
Having established that the lack of pecuniary gain is not an exception to the
application of the law, the Commission next considered the core issue of whether
[Employee] would have a personal or private interest in [the non-profit] that may conflict
with his State job duties.
[Employee]’s Request Letter recognized that he had two potential conflicts of
interest. The first potential conflict was that the [Agency] licenses facilities like one of the
[non-profit’s] programs. Although the [licensure process makes accommodations for an
appeal process], the [Employee] was the ultimate decision-maker regarding whether to
approve/revoke licenses. Ordinarily, the Commission would advise the state official that
they could cure the conflict with an appropriate recusal strategy. A recusal strategy
involves passing the issue (usually some type of decision) creating the conflict to someone
higher up the chain of command. In that way, subordinates do not have to fear making
decisions that may displease their supervisor. However, [Employee was high enough in
the chain of command that he could not pass a matter to another employee because the
employees reported to him]. As a consequence, the Commission decided that the conflict
of interest could not be cured by his recusal.
Having found a conflict of interest, the Commission did not review the second
potential conflict [Employee] described in his Request Letter, expansion of a [grant].
B. State officials may not engage in conduct that may raise suspicion among
The public that they are engaging in conduct contrary to the public trust.
The purpose of the code is to ensure that there is not only no actual violation, but
also not even a “justifiable impression” of a violation. The Commission treats that as an
appearance of impropriety standard. The test is whether a reasonable person,
knowledgeable of all the relevant facts, would still believe that the official’s duties could not
be performed with honesty, integrity and impartiality. Thus, in deciding appearance of
impropriety issues, the Commission looks at the totality of the circumstances. Those
circumstances should be examined within the framework of the Code’s purpose which is to
achieve a balance between a “justifiable impression” that the Code is being violated by an
official, while not “unduly circumscribing” their conduct so that citizens are encouraged to
assume public office and employment.
Having decided that [Employee] would have an actual conflict of interest, the
Commission did not discuss the perception of impropriety.
C. Waivers [of specific provisions of the Code of Conduct] may be granted if
there would be an undue hardship on the State employee or State agency, or the
literal application of the law is not necessary to serve the public purpose.
Having found a conflict of interest, the Commission "may grant a waiver to the
2

specific prohibitions contained therein if the Commission determines that the literal
application of such prohibition in a particular case is not necessary to achieve the public
purposes of this chapter or would result in an undue hardship on any employee, officer,
official or state agency."
(1) "Undue hardship," means "more than required" or is "excessive."
The Commission did not see it’s finding of a conflict of interest to be an undue
hardship on [Employee] or the agency. The denial of his request to be a non-profit Trustee
was not a hardship for the [Agency] because it allowed [Employee] to participate in agency
decisions to the full extent of his statutory powers. In addition, although the Commission’s
decision was likely disappointing, nothing in [Employee]’s Request Letter indicated that he
would suffer a hardship if his waiver request was denied.
(2) Is literal application of the law necessary to serve the public
purpose?
The overall purpose of the Code of Conduct is to instill the public’s confidence in its
government. The statute was designed to protect against self-dealing and its enforcement
is generally the best way to serve the public purpose. None of the facts presented indicated
that the public purpose would be better served by granting [Employee] a waiver to the
State Code of Conduct.
Motion—[Employee]’s acceptance of a position as a Trustee would create a conflict of
interest with his State job duties. A waiver was denied.
23-23 & 23-27 Opinion Violation: On June 20, 2023, the Commission met to discuss the
possibility of initiating a formal Complaint against [two State employees] for a suspected
violation of the Code of Conduct. Specifically, the Commission discussed the expiration of
a previously issued Commission Opinion. Beginning in April 2023, the Public Integrity
Commission (“PIC”) began receiving anonymous phone calls in which the callers alleged
that [an Employee] continued to be employed [with the State], despite the Commission’s
instructions to the contrary. At the conclusion of the June meeting, the Commission
instructed Commission Counsel to draft Complaints for their review at the July meeting.
[The two employees] were both advised of the outcome by letter dated June 21, 2023.
On July 14, 2023, the PIC received a letter from [a legal representative] explaining
the circumstances surrounding [Employee A’s] continued employment at [a State agency].
The letter explained that after the expiration of the previously granted opinion, [Employee
A] remained at [Agency] under a new title and was given new duties that did not overlap
with those of the newly appointed [Division] Director. Consequently, [Employee A] did not
have the authority to sign contracts or award grants; he did not appear in the [Agency]’s
chain of command; and he reported directly to [the Secretary].
During the July 18th meeting, it became clear that the Commission was mistaken
about the [Agency]’s oversight role and their interactions with private facilities. The
Commission had operated under the mistaken assumption that the [Agency] regulated all
[similar] facilities in Delaware. That fact was the primary reason that the Commission
decided that [Employee A] could not work concurrently for the State and for the [private
employer]. However, with further understanding of [Agency]’s role in Delaware, along with
3

[Employee A’s] inability to sign contracts or award grants, the Commission decided to
withdraw its decision to initiate Complaints against both of them.
Despite the best efforts of both the [Agency] and the PIC, it was clear that a simple
miscommunication was the basis of the misunderstandings regarding [Employee A] and his
role at [Agency].
Motion—The Commission withdrew its decision to draft Complaints against [the two
Employees].
23-24—Private Interest
[Employee] worked for [a State agency]. His job duties included [omitted to protect
confidentiality]. During the course of his workday, [Employee] had extensive contact with
[Agency] customers.
[Employee] also owned a [private business] that provided [a product related to his
State job]. His ownership of the [business] predated his employment [with the State]. His
wife ran the business when [Employee] was unavailable.
After [Employee] queried whether it would be possible to set up a booth on
[Agency] property to sell [a product], his supervisors recommended that he obtain an
opinion from the Commission regarding whether his private business created a conflict of
interest with his State job duties.
A. In their official capacity, employees may not review or dispose of matters
if they have a personal or private interest in a matter before them.
“A personal or private interest in a matter is an interest which tends to impair a
person’s independence of judgment in the performance of the person’s duties with respect
to that matter.” ‘Matter’ is defined as “any application, petition, request, business dealing or
transaction of any sort.” When there is a personal or private interest, the official is to
recuse from the outset and even neutral and unbiased statements are prohibited.
[Employee] worked for a State agency that had close ties to his private business.
During the course of his workday, [Employee] had contact with people who [purchased the
product] that was sold by his private business. However, without evidence that [Employee]
was approaching [the Agency]’s customers, the Commission was unwilling to impute such
behavior to him based solely on the fact that he owned a business in a related industry.
Based upon [Employee]’s description of his State job duties, it did not appear that he would
have the opportunity to review and dispose of matters related to his private interest.
B. Employees may not engage in conduct that may raise suspicion among
the public that they are engaging in conduct contrary to the public trust.
The purpose of the code is to ensure that there is not only no actual violation, but
also not even a “justifiable impression” of a violation. The Commission treats that as an
appearance of impropriety standard. The test is whether a reasonable person,
knowledgeable of all the relevant facts, would still believe that the official’s duties could not
be performed with honesty, integrity and impartiality. Thus, in deciding appearance of
4

impropriety issues, the Commission looks at the totality of the circumstances. Those
circumstances should be examined within the framework of the Code’s purpose which is to
achieve a balance between a “justifiable impression” that the Code is being violated by an
official, while not “unduly circumscribing” their conduct so that citizens are encouraged to
assume public office and employment.
[Employee]’s request to open a ‘booth’ may have been made in jest but it was a
perfect example of how mere ownership of a business related to a State employee’s job
duties can create the appearance of impropriety. In [Employee]’s case, it prompted his
supervisors to request this advisory opinion. The Commission does not substantiate
violations of the Code of Conduct based solely on the appearance of impropriety because
courts have said that “it is improper to ascribe evil motives to a public official based only on
suspicion and innuendo.” That holding is consistent with the Delaware Supreme Court
decision which held: absent the existence of a conflict, it would not disqualify an individual
based on an unarticulated concern for the “appearance of impropriety.” It noted that
appearances of impropriety claims have been criticized as being too “imprecise, leading to
ad hoc results.” As a result, the Commission decided that despite [Employee]’s ownership
of a private business in an industry related to his State job duties, the ownership itself, was
not grounds to support a violation of the Code of Conduct.
Motion—[Employee]’s ownership of [a private business in a related industry] did not create
an automatic conflict of interest with his State job duties.
23-19—Regulation Review for Conflicts of Interest: In 2022, the Public Integrity
Commission and [the agency] worked together to ensure that portions of the [the agency]’s
proposed administrative regulation were consistent with the ethical standards set forth in
the State Code of Conduct (the ethics laws). The resulting effort was [a specific regulation].
The [agency]’s current regulatory scheme contemplates two types [of activities].
[One type of regulation limits the number of attendees for a particular activity. The other
type of regulation does not limit attendees].
The [agency] was confronted with the issue of how to apply the existing regulation
to [a hybrid activity]. [The request letter defined each type of activity and drew a parallel
between the hybrid activity and another activity that did not have limitations on the number
of attendees].
APPLICABLE STATUTES:
A. 29 Del. C. §5805:
In their official capacity, a state employee, state officer or state official may
not review or dispose of matters if they have a personal or private interest in
a matter before them.
“A personal or private interest in a matter is an interest which tends to impair a
person’s independence of judgment in the performance of the person’s duties with respect
to that matter.” A person has a personal or private interest when they, or a close relative,
have a financial interest in a private enterprise.” ‘Matter’ is defined as “any application,
petition, request, business dealing or transaction of any sort.” A personal or private interest
5

in a matter is an interest which tends to impair a person’s independence of judgment in the
performance of the person’s duties with respect to that matter.” When there is a personal
or private interest, the official is to recuse from the outset and even neutral and unbiased
statements are prohibited.
B. Employees may not engage in conduct that may raise suspicion among the
public that they are engaging in conduct contrary to the public trust.
The purpose of the code is to ensure that there is not only no actual violation, but
also not even a “justifiable impression” of a violation. The Commission treats that as an
appearance of impropriety standard. The test is whether a reasonable person,
knowledgeable of all the relevant facts, would still believe that the official’s duties could not
be performed with honesty, integrity and impartiality. Thus, in deciding appearance of
impropriety issues, the Commission looks at the totality of the circumstances. Those
circumstances should be examined within the framework of the Code’s purpose which is to
achieve a balance between a “justifiable impression” that the Code is being violated by an
official, while not “unduly circumscribing” their conduct so that citizens are encouraged to
assume public office and employment.
C. State employees may not accept other employment if acceptance may
result in:
(1) impaired judgment in performing official duties:
To avoid impaired judgment in performing official duties, State employees may not
review or dispose of matters if they have a personal or private interest.
(2) preferential treatment to any person:
The next concern addressed by the statute is to ensure co-workers and colleagues
are not placed in a position to make decisions that may result in preferential treatment to
any person. State Employees may not represent or assist a private organization before
their own agency.
(3) official decisions outside official channels:
State Employees are entitled to a strong presumption of honesty and integrity.
(4) any adverse effect on the public’s confidence in the integrity of its
government:
The purpose of the code is to ensure that there is not only no actual violation, but
also not even a “justifiable impression” of a violation. The Commission treats this provision
as an appearance of impropriety standard. The test is whether a reasonable person,
knowledgeable of all the relevant facts, would still believe that the State duties could not be
performed with honesty, integrity and impartiality.
ANALYSIS
The regulations related to [Activity A] are more stringent than those that apply to
[Activity B] because the risk of creating a conflict of interest is greatest in the context of
[Activity A]. Reasons for the heightened risk included, but were not limited to, [being paid
6

for their participation, the influence of outside organizations and the development of
personal friendships through repeated contact. In mitigation of those possible conflicts,
[the agency] emphasized that [personnel] would not be paid and all of the other restrictions
related to [Activity A] would be applied. Those regulations included [then followed a 10-
item list of restrictions that are omitted here for confidentiality].
The Commission agreed with [the agency]’s analysis that in the context of a [hybrid
activity], allowing 100% [participation], while also imposing the stricter safeguards of
[Activity A], was unlikely to result in the development of personal and private interests
between a school coach and their student athletes.
Motion: Attendance as described would not create a conflict of interest.
23-17—Private Interest/Waiver Request
[Employee] was hired as a Program Administrator for the State. His job
responsibilities included contract management, workforce development, technical
assistance and resource development. Some of [Employee]’s job duties included
administering [a federal grant] and ccompiling federal reporting criteria and fiscal
management.
Prior to working for the State, [Employee] was a [contracted vendor under a federal
grant]. He was told that he would no longer be able to work under the grant once he
became a State employee. According to [Employee], [the agency] asked him to re-apply to
be a provider under the program because they were having difficulty finding program
providers. If allowed to work under the grant, [Employee] would reach out to school, club
and community recreational sports teams to provide training to coaches and/or to conduct
training classes. Locations would include community centers, churches, gyms and fields
across the state.
[Employee] asked the Commission whether he could contract to work under a grant
administered by his State agency. If the Commission determined that [Employee]’s
proposed work under the grant would create a conflict of interest, he requested a waiver.
A. In their official capacity, employees may not review or dispose of matters
if they have a personal or private interest in a matter before them.
“A personal or private interest in a matter is an interest which tends to impair a
person’s independence of judgment in the performance of the person’s duties with respect
to that matter.” ‘Matter’ is defined as “any application, petition, request, business dealing or
transaction of any sort.” When there is a personal or private interest, the official is to
recuse from the outset and even neutral and unbiased statements are prohibited.
[Employee] was a contract manager for the agency but he did not administer the
[specific] grant at issue. Therefore, it was unlikely that [Employee] would be asked to
7

review and dispose of matters related to the federal grant while performing his State job
duties.
B. Employees may not engage in conduct that may raise suspicion among
the public that they are engaging in conduct contrary to the public trust.
The purpose of the code is to ensure that there is not only no actual violation, but
also not even a “justifiable impression” of a violation. The Commission treats that as an
appearance of impropriety standard. The test is whether a reasonable person,
knowledgeable of all the relevant facts, would still believe that the official’s duties could not
be performed with honesty, integrity and impartiality. Thus, in deciding appearance of
impropriety issues, the Commission looks at the totality of the circumstances. Those
circumstances should be examined within the framework of the Code’s purpose which is to
achieve a balance between a “justifiable impression” that the Code is being violated by an
official, while not “unduly circumscribing” their conduct so that citizens are encouraged to
assume public office and employment.
The Code of Conduct was created to prevent conflicts of interest such as the one
before the Commission. [Employee] was a contract manager, intimately familiar with the
Division’s bargaining tactics, funding and procedures. Even if he did not personally
manage the federal grant, a contract with his own agency was likely to create an
appearance of impropriety.
C. Waivers may be granted if there would be an undue hardship on the State
employee or State agency, or the literal application of the law is not
necessary to serve the public purpose.
Having found an appearance of impropriety, the Commission next considered a
waiver. Originally, [Employee’s supervisor] was scheduled to appear at the meeting via
Zoom. However, shortly before the meeting began, [the supervisor] sent Commission
Counsel an email stating she would be unable to attend. In the email she described her
basis for requesting a waiver. The email was read into the record in its entirety during the
meeting.
(1) "Undue hardship," means "more than required" or is
"excessive."
The Division did not seek providers through the traditional Request For Proposals
process and did little beyond word-of-mouth inquiries to locate a new provider. Given
those circumstances, the Commission decided that the Division had not established an
undue hardship. Therefore, the request for a waiver on this basis was denied.
(2) Is literal application of the law necessary to serve the public
purpose?
The overall purpose of the Code of Conduct is to instill the public’s confidence in its
government. The statute was designed to protect against self-dealing and its enforcement
is generally the best way to serve the public purpose. While publication of a waiver
somewhat mitigates speculation about inside dealing, it is not a substitute for upholding
appropriate limitations on a state employee’s ability to obtain a state contract.
8

As noted above, the statute is designed to prohibit self-dealing amongst State
employees. The fact that the Division told [Employee] that he could not keep the grant
contract before they hired him was acknowledgement of the fact that the Division was
aware of the negative perception created when a State contract/grant is given to a State
employee. Nothing submitted to the Commission in support of the waiver overcame the
statutory presumption that enforcement of the State Code of Conduct was the best way to
serve the public purpose.
Motion—[Employee] could not contract with his own agency and the Commission declined
to issue a waiver to allow him to do so.
23-14 Complaint
I. PROCEDURE
Any person may file a sworn Complaint alleging violations of Title 29, Delaware
Code, ch. 58. The ‘complaint’ was not notarized. The Commission decided not to dismiss
the complaint based solely on the procedural defect, reasoning that the complaint could
easily be notarized and re-submitted if necessary. In addition, the Commission wanted to
take the time to address the concerns set forth in the letter.
A. Jurisdiction
The Commission’s jurisdiction is limited to interpreting Title 29, Del. C., Ch. 58. It
may only act if it has jurisdiction over the party charged and jurisdiction over the
Complaint’s substance.
1. Personal Jurisdiction
[Employee] is a state employee and as a result, falls within the Commission’s
jurisdiction.
2. Subject Matter Jurisdiction
The Commission can only address alleged violations of "this chapter"-Title 29, Ch.
58. The letter stated that [Employee] violated the Code of Conduct by voting on a matter in
which he had a personal or private interest.
II. FACTS
The letter was received in the PIC’s offices on April 12, 2023, after initially being
delivered to the wrong address. [Employee] was employed by the State [in an
administrative role]. [A request for proposals (“RFP”) was initiated by the agency to
provide services to the public]. Two groups submitted proposals for the bid.”
“[Bidder #2] ultimately won the contract based on a review committee scoring matrix
of the proposal. The subjective opinion of the bid tabulation committee was that [Bidder
#2’s] proposal was more creative and offered a better financial gain for the State. The bid
tabulation committee consisted of 7 [state] employees, [including the subject of the
9

complaint].
“[Complainant stated that employee had a ‘personal or private interest’ in [Bidder
#2] because [Bidder #2] posted on …Instagram a picture of [Employee’s] daughter
[working at their facility]”
Upon receipt of the letter, Commission Counsel reached out to the Deputy Attorney
General representing [the agency], who in turn reached out to [Employee]. According to
[Employee], his daughter worked at [Bidder #2’s business] during the summers of 2020,
2021 and 2022. Since then, [she] occasionally worked when needed but was not an
employee of [Bidder #2]. [Employee’s] daughter was a full-time teacher and in summer
2023, she would be working [at a different location].
The agency’s Deputy Attorney General stated that “[t]he RFP process …was not
unusual; it followed the normal contract bidding process. Prior to the RFP, [Employee] did
not know the owners or principals of [Bidder #2]. [Employee] was one of the six or seven
[agency] employees who worked on the RFP. [Employee] worked with another [agency]
employee in evaluating the bidders' financials to ensure that [it] was fiscally sound and to
evaluate the proposed revenue.”
III. LAW
A. In their official capacity, employees may not review or dispose of matters if
they have a personal or private interest in a matter before them. 29 Del. C. §
5805(a)(1).
A personal or private interest in a matter is an interest which tends to impair a
person’s independence of judgment in the performance of the person’s duties with respect
to that matter.” As a matter of law, a person has a personal or private interest if any
decision “with respect to the matter would result in a financial benefit or detriment to accrue
to the person or a close relative to a greater extent” than others similarly situated or if “the
person or a close relative has a financial interest in a private enterprise which would be
affected” by a decision on the matter to a greater or lesser degree than others similarly
situated. ‘Close relative’ is defined as “a person's parents, spouse, children (natural or
adopted) and siblings of the whole and half-blood.”
Obviously, [Employee]’s daughter was a family member. However, it was not clear
from the letter whether [Employee] had a conflict of interest (through his daughter) when he
was actively reviewing the bids. This Commission has previously decided that using past
conflicts of interest to require recusal ad infinitum is contrary to the purpose of the Code of
Conduct which is to achieve a balance between the State’s interests and [Employee]’s
restrictions. “In our democratic form of government, it is both necessary and desirable that
all citizens should be encouraged to assume public office and employment, and that,
therefore, the activities of officers and employees of the State should not be unduly
circumscribed.”
Requiring State employees to recuse themselves from every decision that involves
a past conflict of interest would be unduly burdensome and unnecessary. At the time of the
review, [Employee]’s adult daughter had completed her summer employment and had
returned to her full-time job. Therefore, she no longer had a financial interest in [Bidder #2].
It could be argued that [employee’s daughter] had a financial interest in [Bidder #2] on the
days that she ‘filled-in’ during the Fall of 2022. In order for that conflict to be imputed to
10

[Employee], it would have to be proven that [Employee] knew, on the specific days he
worked on the RFP, that his daughter was working for [Bidder #2], thus affecting his official
judgment.
The Commission decided that the circumstances surrounding the allegation of a
conflict of interest were too attenuated to support a finding of a violation of the Code of
Conduct.
B. Each state employee…shall endeavor to pursue a course of conduct which
will not raise suspicion among the public that such official is engaging in acts
which are in violation of the public trust and which will not reflect unfavorably
upon the government. 29 Del. C. § 5806(a).
This provision of the Code of Conduct prohibits conduct violating the public trust.
This is basically an appearance of impropriety test. The test is whether a reasonable
person, knowledgeable of all the relevant facts, would still believe that the official’s duties
could not be performed with honesty, integrity and impartiality. In deciding appearance of
impropriety issues, the Commission looks at the totality of the circumstances. Those
circumstances should be examined within the framework of the Code’s purpose which is to
achieve a balance between a “justifiable impression” that the Code is being violated by an
official, while not “unduly circumscribing” their conduct so that citizens are encouraged to
assume public office and employment.
The wording in this section of the Code of Conduct contemplates a current conflict
by the use of the verbiage “is engaging in acts” which “are” in violation of the public trust.
Nothing in the statute indicated that a current appearance of impropriety could be created
by a past conflict of interest. Or, in other words, the appearance of impropriety must be
contemporaneous with the conflict of interest. As a result, this allegation was also
dismissed.
Motion—Dismissed for failure to state a claim.
23-11—Personal Interest: (Commissioner Chaney dissented from the decision in this
matter): [Employee] worked for a three-person, non-merit, State agency. The [Agency]
wanted to hire an intern to fill an open casual/seasonal position. Neither the State of
Delaware Recruitment Procedures Manual, nor the Delaware Code required this position to
be posted. [Candidate] was dating [Employee]’s adult son. [Employee] did not believe it
was a conflict of interest for her to hire [Candidate] because they were not related by blood
or marriage. [Employee] notified the [Agency]’s interns about the possibility of a paid,
casual/seasonal position and [Candidate] was the only intern interested in “the limited
hours and low pay.”
[Candidate]’s job interview was conducted by the [Agency] Chairperson, Vice-
Chairperson, Personnel Committee Chair and two staff persons. [Employee] “excused
herself from being a part of the interview process, as she was known to the applicant.”
After reviewing her resume and application, the panel interviewed [Candidate] and decided
that she met the job requirements and that her desire to learn more about the “disability,
exceptionality community [was] admirable.” “The decision to offer the position to
[Candidate] was the joint decision of the Chair, Vice-Chair and Personnel Committee Chair,
11

with positive input from [Agency] staff.”
[Candidate] would be working under the supervision of the Office Manager.
[Candidate]’s hours, duties and pay would be monitored by the Office Manager and
Administrative Assistant. [Employee] would approve items brought to her by [the other two
employees], such as timesheets and staff evaluations.
[Employee] asked the Commission if it would be a conflict of interest for her to hire
[Candidate].
A. In their official capacity, employees may not review or dispose of matters
if they have a personal or private interest in a matter before them.
A personal or private interest in a matter is an interest which tends to impair a
person’s independence of judgment in the performance of the person’s duties with respect
to that matter.” As a matter of law, a person has a personal or private interest if any
decision “with respect to the matter would result in a financial benefit or detriment to accrue
to the person or a close relative to a greater extent” than others similarly situated or if “the
person or a close relative has a financial interest in a private enterprise which would be
affected” by a decision on the matter to a greater or lesser degree than others similarly
situated. ‘Close relative’ is defined as “a person's parents, spouse, children (natural or
adopted) and siblings of the whole and half-blood.”
A personal or private interest is not limited to narrow definitions such as “close
relatives” and “financial interest.” Rather, it recognizes that a State official can have a
“personal or private interest” outside those limited parameters. It is a codification of the
common law restriction on government officials. When there is a personal or private
interest, the official is to recuse from the outset and even neutral and unbiased statements
are prohibited.
[Employee] supported her request by noting that “there [was] a Personnel Manual
to ensure checks and balances [were] in place to avoid any appearance of favoritism or
personal bias in favor of, or against, [Candidate], with input from the Chair of the [Agency]
and Personnel Committee Chair of the [Agency].”
Setting aside the [Agency]’s Personnel Manual, which was completely separate
from the State Code of Conduct, [Candidate] was not a ‘close relative’. As a result,
[Employee] did not have a conflict of interest as a matter of law. However, the Commission
next considered whether she had a conflict of interest as a matter of fact. The Commission
considered the facts in support of a conflict of interest: the job was not posted, limiting the
number of applicants; [Employee] felt that she knew [Candidate] well enough that she
recused herself from the interview process but not the hiring process; the proposed recusal
strategy was flawed because all the employees involved in the recusal ultimately reported
to [Employee]. The factors mitigating against a conflict of interest included: the job was
part-time, low-paying and in a career field in which the State has struggled to hire.
The Commission decided that [Candidate] could be hired to fill the casual/seasonal
position as long as she ultimately reported to the Chair of the [Agency] Personnel
Committee. That person was not within [Employee]’s chain of command because they
were an appointed member of the council, rather than an employee of the State. In that
way, [Employee] would not be required to review and dispose of matters related to
[Candidate] while performing her official job duties.
12

B. Employees may not engage in conduct that may raise suspicion among
the public that they are engaging in conduct contrary to the public trust.
The purpose of the code is to ensure that there is not only no actual violation, but
also not even a “justifiable impression” of a violation. The Commission treats that as an
appearance of impropriety standard. The test is whether a reasonable person,
knowledgeable of all the relevant facts, would still believe that the official’s duties could not
be performed with honesty, integrity and impartiality. Thus, in deciding appearance of
impropriety issues, the Commission looks at the totality of the circumstances. Those
circumstances are examined within the framework of the Code’s purpose which is to
achieve a balance between a “justifiable impression” that the Code is being violated by an
official, while not “unduly circumscribing” their conduct so that citizens are encouraged to
assume public office and employment.
As discussed above, there was no conflict of interest as a matter of law. However,
there were two competing State interests that had to be considered before determining
whether [Employee] could hire [Candidate]. The Commission first considered the State’s
interest in not unduly limiting the conduct of (prospective) State employees. [Candidate]
was dating [Employee]’s adult son who did not live at home. That fact reduced the amount
of exposure [Candidate] would have to [Employee] outside of work hours. In addition, the
Commission felt that concern could be addressed by having [Candidate] report to someone
outside of [Employee]’s chain of command. Second, the Commission considered the
State’s interests in hiring qualified employees and being fully staffed. [Candidate] wanted
to accept a part-time job that was, by all accounts, low-paying and had limited prospects for
advancement. [Employee] stated that despite the fact that the job was not posted, she did
not anticipate having any other candidates for the position. Balancing all the interests the
Commission decided that the appearance of impropriety could be eliminated by having
[Candidate] report to the Chair of the Personnel Committee.
Motion: [Employee] could hire [Candidate] as long as [Candidate] reported to the Chair of
the [Agency] Personnel Committee.
23-09-—Personal or Private Interest (Waiver Granted) Because a waiver was granted,
the opinion is published in its entirety. Footnotes were omitted for formatting purposes:
VIA EMAIL March 16, 2023
Hearing and Decision By: Hon. F. Gary Simpson (Chair); Hon. Rourke Moore (Vice-
Chair) (virtual); Ron Chaney (Vice-Chair). Commissioners: Andrew T. Manus (virtual),
Marjorie Biles, Judge (Ret.) Alex Smalls.
Dear Dr. Carson,
13

Thank you for attending the February 15, 2023, Commission meeting which you
attended via Zoom videoconference. After consideration of the relevant facts and
circumstances, the Commission decided that your employment contract contains an
inherent conflict of interest. Consequently, the Commission is granting a waiver to all you
to engage in collective bargaining on behalf of the District. The Commission’s reasoning is
set forth below.
I. FACTS
You are the Superintendent and Executive Secretary of the Board of Education of
the Sussex County Vocational Technical School District ("Board" or “District”). You are
both an employee of the District and its Chief Executive Officer (“CEO”). In your written
submission, you stated that “[a]ll matter[s are] ultimately [your] responsibility.” One of your
job responsibilities is to make recommendations to the Board regarding collective
bargaining. This spring, the Board and teachers will be negotiating a new collective
bargaining agreement. The existing agreement expires on June 30, 2023. It is your job to
obtain the “most beneficial contract, which balances financial, operational and other
interests.”
Given the current labor market, you anticipate that the District will need to raise
existing pay scales to attract and retain teachers. Those increases, if approved, will have a
direct effect on you because your employment contract ties increases in teacher’s salaries
to increases in your salary. The result is that you cannot recommend an increase in
teacher’s salaries without also recommending an increase in your own salary.
In deciding whether to recommend pay raises, you are required by statute to
consider the following factors:
(1) The interests and welfare of the public.
(2) Comparison of the wages, salaries, benefits, hours and conditions of
employment of the employees involved in the binding interest arbitration
proceedings with the wages, salaries, benefits, hours and conditions of employment
of other employees performing the same or similar services or requiring similar
skills under similar working conditions in the same community and in comparable
communities and with other employees generally in the same community and in
comparable communities.
(3) The overall compensation presently received by the employees inclusive of
direct wages, salary, vacations, holidays, excused leaves, insurance and pensions,
medical and hospitalization benefits, the continuity and stability of employment and
all other benefits received.
(4) Stipulations of the parties.
(5) The lawful authority of the public-school employer.
(6) The financial ability of the public-school employer based on existing revenues,
to meet the costs of any proposed settlements… .
(7) Such other factors not confined to the foregoing which are normally or
traditionally taken into consideration in the determination of wages, hours and
conditions of employment through voluntary collective bargaining, mediation,
binding interest arbitration or otherwise between parties, in public service or in
private employment.
The determination of what the Board has the financial ability to pay is calculated
primarily by the Board's business manager, Kristen Hatfield. However, you believe it will
14

be necessary for you to have some involvement in “negotiating against the union” and you
cannot delegate your responsibility because the matter requires your professional
experience and affects the District’s overall budget. You disclosed this information to the
Board on February 8, 2023.
You asked the Commission if the fact that your pay increases are predicated on
increases in teacher’s salaries, creates a conflict of interest while performing your job
duties.
II. APPLICATION OF THE FACTS TO THE LAW
A. In their official capacity, employees may not review or dispose of matters
if they have a personal or private interest in a matter before them.
“A personal or private interest in a matter is an interest which tends to impair a
person’s independence of judgment in the performance of the person’s duties with respect
to that matter.” ‘Matter’ is defined as “any application, petition, request, business dealing or
transaction of any sort.” When there is a personal or private interest, the official is to
recuse from the outset and even neutral and unbiased statements are prohibited.
Your employment contract created an inherent conflict of interest by tying increases
in your personal compensation to increases in teacher pay. Although your decision
regarding whether to recommend any pay increases is limited by the factors set forth
above, the Commission cannot reach any other conclusion than it is a conflict of interest for
you to review and dispose of a matter (collective bargaining) in which you have a personal
interest, your compensation. The District’s decision to tie your compensation to that of its
teachers was likely based on a laudable desire to keep administrative salaries
proportionate to that of its teachers. However, the end result is that if teachers receive a
pay increase, so do you. While the result would be through no fault of your own, it would
still constitute a violation of the State Code of Conduct.
Because you are bound by your employment contract to negotiate collective
bargaining agreements on behalf of the District, the Commission decided to GRANT you a
waiver to allow you to participate in this year’s collective bargaining negotiations and any
follow-up matters that are a direct result of those negotiations. However, the Commission
recommends that the provision of your employment contract that links your compensation
to that of the District’s teachers be removed. Nor should your compensation be tied to any
employee of the District over whom you have supervisory power.
B. Employees may not engage in conduct that may raise suspicion among
the public that they are engaging in conduct contrary to the public trust.
The purpose of the code is to ensure that there is not only no actual violation, but
also not even a “justifiable impression” of a violation. The Commission treats that as an
appearance of impropriety standard. The test is whether a reasonable person,
knowledgeable of all the relevant facts, would still believe that the official’s duties could not
be performed with honesty, integrity and impartiality. Thus, in deciding appearance of
impropriety issues, the Commission looks at the totality of the circumstances. Those
circumstances should be examined within the framework of the Code’s purpose which is to
achieve a balance between a “justifiable impression” that the Code is being violated by an
official, while not “unduly circumscribing” their conduct so that citizens are encouraged to
assume public office and employment.
15

The appearance of impropriety is mitigated by the fact that you are bound by the
terms of your employment contract and are not acting of your own volition. The statutory
requirements that apply to collective bargaining also lessen the appearance of impropriety.
However, as you correctly recognized by bringing this matter to our attention, it may appear
inappropriate for you to negotiate an agreement in which you also benefit.
III. CONCLUSION
The Commission grants you a waiver to allow you to participate in this year’s
collective bargaining negotiations. The District should revise your employment contract to
remove the connection between your pay and the pay of employees you supervise. If you
have any questions, please feel free to contact us.
Sincerely,
/s/ F. Gary Simpson
Hon. F. Gary Simpson
Chair
Motion: Dr. Carson’s employment contract created a conflict of interest with his collective
bargaining job duties. The Commission granted a waiver so that the District could proceed
with negotiations.

23-06—Personal or Private Interest: Commission Counsel received an anonymous
phone call stating that a Deputy Director of [a State agency] had “hired her niece” through
a temporary staffing service. Counsel instructed the caller how to file a formal complaint
and reached out to the Director of the [Agency] to see if he could confirm the facts of the
inquiry. The caller never filed a formal complaint. [The Director] looked into the matter and
provided Commission Counsel with information related to the allegation.
[The Deputy Director] had, in fact, hired her second cousin and two of the cousin’s
friends to work at [Agency] through a temporary staffing service in September 2020, when
the Division was overwhelmed with [work]. The [employees] were still working for [the
Agency] through the staffing service because the labor market had made it difficult for the
State to recruit and retain staff.
1. In their official capacity, employees may not review or dispose of matters if
they have a personal or private interest in a matter before them.
A personal or private interest in a matter is an interest which tends to impair a
person’s independence of judgment in the performance of the person’s duties with respect
to that matter.” As a matter of law, a person has a personal or private interest if any
decision “with respect to the matter would result in a financial benefit or detriment to accrue
to the person or a close relative to a greater extent” than others similarly situated or if “the
person or a close relative has a financial interest in a private enterprise which would be
affected” by a decision on the matter to a greater or lesser degree than others similarly
situated. Close relative is defined as “a person’s parents, spouse, children (natural or
adopted) and siblings of the whole and half-blood.” Obviously, “cousins” did not fall within
the definition. When the language is clear, a statute must be held to mean what is clearly
expressed. As a result, [the Deputy Director] did not have a conflict of interest as a matter
of law because the family relationship of ‘cousin’ was too distant.
However, personal and private interests are not limited to narrow definitions such
as “close relatives” and “financial interest.” Rather, the law recognizes that a State official
can have a “personal or private interest” outside those limited parameters. It is a
codification of the common law restriction on government officials. When there is a
personal or private interest, the official is to recuse from the outset and even neutral and
unbiased statements are prohibited. Under the common law, and its codification, “the
decision as to whether a particular interest is sufficient to disqualify is necessarily a factual
one and depends upon the circumstances of the particular case.”
The Commission lacked sufficient information to determine if [the Deputy Director]
had a conflict of interest as a matter of fact because the closeness of her relationship with
her second cousin was unknown. The Commission was also aware, through other
requests for advisory opinions, that the [Agency] was overwhelmed during the COVID-19
shutdown in early 2020. As a consequence, temporary staffing agencies were used to
bolster existing [Agency] staff. Given those circumstances, the Commission decided not to
pursue the verbal allegations shared by the anonymous caller.
18

However, the Commission reminded [the Director] that the same ethical standards
that applied to hiring permanent employees, also applied to hiring temporary staff. Anyone
with a relationship to one of the applicants should not be involved in hiring, disciplining or
supervising that applicant. While it was too late to apply the proper standard to the hiring
process, the Commission recommended that [the Deputy Director] be removed from her
cousin’s chain of command. The cousin should report to someone in the agency who was
not subject to [the Deputy Director]’s supervision. In that way, the supervising employee
did not have to fear possible retaliation for decisions made about [the Deputy Director]’s
cousin.
2. Employees may not engage in conduct that may raise suspicion among the
public that they are engaging in conduct contrary to the public trust.
The purpose of the code is to ensure that there is not only no actual violation, but
also not even a “justifiable impression” of a violation. The Commission treats that as an
appearance of impropriety standard. The test is whether a reasonable person,
knowledgeable of all the relevant facts, would still believe that the official’s duties could not
be performed with honesty, integrity and impartiality. Thus, in deciding appearance of
impropriety issues, the Commission looks at the totality of the circumstances. Those
circumstances should be examined within the framework of the Code’s purpose which is to
achieve a balance between a “justifiable impression” that the Code is being violated by an
official, while not “unduly circumscribing” their conduct so that citizens are encouraged to
assume public office and employment.
At least one employee was aware of a familial relationship between [the Deputy
Director] and her second cousin. Although the staffing agency stood as an intermediary
between [the Deputy Director] and her relative, it was unlikely that they were involved in the
day-to-day supervision of the relative. Consequently, the best way to remove the
appearance of impropriety was for the cousin to report to someone outside [the Deputy
Director]’s chain of command. The revised reporting structure will assure the public that

cousin.

23-01—Personal Interest--(Commissioner Smalls disclosed that he knew [the applicant]
professionally. No motion for recusal).
[Two elected officials were on a Board that awarded grants]. Before participating in
any votes, the [applicants] “[wanted] to clarify the ethical procedure for voting on funding
applications filed by an individual or organization that may have contributed to one of our
previous political campaigns.” [They] asked the Commission whether knowledge of an
applicant’s prior campaign contribution created a conflict of interest when voting on a
matter directly affecting the contributor.
A. In their official capacity, employees may not review or dispose of matters if
they have a personal or private interest in a matter before them.
A personal or private interest in a matter is an interest which tends to impair a
person’s independence of judgment in the performance of the person’s duties with respect
to that matter.” When there is a personal or private interest, the official is to recuse from
the outset and even neutral and unbiased statements are prohibited.
22

When considering the influence of campaign contributions, the U.S. Supreme Court
concluded “…that independent expenditures, including those made by corporations, do not
give rise to corruption or the appearance of corruption. That speakers may have influence
over or access to elected officials does not mean that those officials are corrupt. And the
appearance of influence or access will not cause the electorate to lose faith in this
democracy.”
In states where members of the judiciary are elected, judges are to consider the
size of the contribution relative to others similarly situated. “Political contributions are for
the purpose of obtaining or being considered for a government legal engagement or
appointment by a judge if, but for the desire to be considered for the legal engagement or
appointment, the lawyer or law firm would not have made or solicited the contributions. The
purpose may be determined by an examination of the circumstances in which the
contributions occur. Those factors may include among others that the contribution or
solicitation was made to further a political, social, or economic interest or because of an
existing personal, family, or professional relationship with a candidate.
Outright bans on campaign contribution directed towards specific classes of citizens
are usually, but not always, prohibited by the First Amendment. In states that have
successfully enacted laws which limit or ban campaign contributions by a specific segment
of the population (i.e., lobbyists) the remedy at law is to change the campaign finance

automatically trigger a conflict-of-interest. However, the donation must be considered in
real world circumstances which measure the size, timing and frequency of donations. It

their independence of judgment.

The purpose of the code is to ensure that there is not only no actual violation, but
also not even a “justifiable impression” of a violation. The Commission treats that as an
appearance of impropriety standard. The test is whether a reasonable person,
knowledgeable of all the relevant facts, would still believe that the official’s duties could not

official, while not “unduly circumscribing” their conduct so that citizens are encouraged to

campaign contribution created a personal interest capable of affecting the public official’s
judgment. Furthermore, the grant review committees added an additional layer of formal

interest, the person files a written statement with the Commission fully
